analysis.one_liner: Requires fracking operations to test nearby drinking water for contamination and report results to a public database.
analysis.headline: The fracking water-testing bill was introduced with 21 House Democrats and referred to committee, which has taken no action since November 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require oil, gas, and geothermal drilling operations that use hydraulic fracturing (fracking) to test underground drinking water near their sites for contamination and report the results to the EPA within two weeks. It would add testing before fracking starts, every six months during operations, and annually for five years afterward, and would require the EPA to put the results into a public, searchable online database. States could only run their own underground injection programs if they enforce these testing rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents who live near fracking sites and rely on underground sources of drinking water. They would get regular, lab-certified testing of their water and the ability to look up results by ZIP code on the EPA website. If contamination shows up, they would have documented evidence sooner, rather than finding out through symptoms or their own testing. States and the EPA would also gain better data on whether fracking is contaminating drinking water.

how_it_helps.text: Requires fracking operators to test underground sources of drinking water within half a mile (or up to a mile) of their sites, before fracking begins, every six months during operations, and annually for five years after shutdown.
Testing must be done by EPA-certified laboratories and cover hazardous substances the EPA determines would indicate fracking-related damage.
Operators must report results to the EPA within two weeks, and the EPA must maintain a public, searchable database that residents can search by ZIP code.
States could keep primary enforcement of underground injection programs only if they prohibit fracking-related injection unless the operator agrees to the testing and reporting requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and geothermal companies that use fracking. They would pay for recurring testing at EPA-certified labs and for reporting, and contamination results would become public, which could increase cleanup costs, regulatory scrutiny, and legal liability.

drawbacks.text: The exemption is defined by access: sites with no accessible underground source of drinking water within one mile are exempt, and the bill defines 'accessible' as water the operator can reasonably reach, which leaves room for narrower testing than the headline suggests.
The bill requires testing and reporting, not prevention: an operator could legally frack and report contamination afterward, so it produces evidence rather than stopping contamination directly.
Recurring testing would add compliance costs for fracking operators, which industry could pass on through higher energy prices or fewer wells.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is straightforward: regular, independent testing with results the public can actually see, closing a gap created when fracking was exempted from most Safe Drinking Water Act permitting. The main costs fall on operators, and the monitoring-only design means contamination can still happen; the bill makes it visible rather than illegal. The access-based exemption and the operator-controlled definition of 'accessible' water are the weakest parts, but they narrow rather than erase the core benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in November 2025 and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has not scheduled any hearing or vote, and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 18, 2025 by Rep. Janice Schakowsky with 20 Democratic cosponsors.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled.

The bill would amend the Safe Drinking Water Act to require fracking operators to test underground sources of drinking water, report results to the EPA within two weeks, and allow public searches of the results by ZIP code.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and geothermal fracking operators are better off so far: the current rules still require no routine testing or public reporting of drinking water contamination near fracking sites, and nothing has changed. Residents near fracking sites continue to bear the risk without the data the bill would have produced.

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 18, 2025 and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: 20 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republicans signed on.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Accepted the referral on November 18, 2025 and has taken no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 20 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has joined, and the Republican-led committee has not moved the bill.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and geothermal companies that use fracking
industries.note: They would bear recurring lab testing and reporting costs, and public contamination results would create regulatory and legal exposure they do not currently face because fracking is largely exempt from Safe Drinking Water Act permitting. Industry opposition to fracking-related drinking water rules is well documented outside the congressional record.
The bill requires testing by EPA-certified labs, roughly doubling to tripling the testing cycle at every fracking site near drinking water, which would be new paid business for those laboratories.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and no committee action more than a year after referral, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing, markup, or floor vote in a Republican-run House. Its most probable path is to die in committee when the Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
